## Frequently asked questions
What are the annual compliances for an Indian subsidiary of a foreign company?
Statutory audit and AGM, financial statements and annual return with MCA, income-tax return and transfer-pricing report, the FLA return to RBI by 15 July, monthly GST and TDS, payroll filings, and FC-GPR within 30 days of any share issue.

Does an Indian subsidiary need a resident director?
Yes. Every Indian company needs at least one director who has stayed in India for 182 days or more in the financial year.

Can you report to us in US GAAP or IFRS?
Yes. We close the Indian books under Ind AS or Indian GAAP for statutory purposes and map them to the parent's US GAAP or IFRS reporting each month.

Can you do the accounting and the statutory audit?
No — an auditor must be independent of the accounting. We handle accounting and compliance and work with your appointed statutory auditor.

India tax

# India tax for foreign companies — get paid without overpaying

Your Indian customer wants a TRC, “Form 10F” and a no-PE declaration, or is deducting 20% from your invoice. We sort out the paperwork, apply your treaty, and tell you when — and whether — you need to file in India.

Ask about India tax
hello@durgeshchavda.com

Talk it through first — free. Book a 15-minute intro call with Durgesh to scope your requirement, timeline and fee.Book a free 15-min intro

## Foreign vendors paid by Indian customers

- Indian payers must withhold tax on many payments to non-residents under section 393(2) of the Income-tax Act, 2025 — royalties and fees for technical services at 20% (plus surcharge and cess) under domestic law.

- Your tax treaty usually cuts that to 10–15%, or to nil for business profits where you have no permanent establishment in India — but only with the right documents: a tax residency certificate, Form 41 (formerly Form 10F), a no-PE declaration and often a PAN.

- The payer files Form 145 and, for most payments, a CA certificate in Form 146 before remitting.

- We prepare your pack once a year and explain it to your Indian customers’ finance teams. Guide: Form 41, TRC and the no-PE declaration.

## Permanent establishment reviews

- Staff, contractors or an office in India can create a taxable presence — a permanent establishment — even without an Indian entity.

- India also taxes non-residents with a significant economic presence (₹2 crore of payments or 3 lakh users), though a treaty’s PE rules generally prevail.

- We review how your people, contracts and servers touch India and suggest fixes. See hiring in India without an entity.

## Do you need to file in India?

- A foreign company with income taxable in India generally files an Indian return.

- The exception: if its only Indian income is dividends, certain interest, royalties or fees for technical services and tax was withheld at no less than the domestic rates. If your customer applied a lower treaty rate, the exemption usually doesn’t apply — a common surprise.

- Refunds of excess withholding, lower-withholding certificates (Form 128) and PAN applications for foreign companies are routine work for us.

## GST for foreign SaaS and digital services

Selling online services to Indian consumers or unregistered businesses? You likely need a simplified GST registration and monthly returns; sales to GST-registered businesses are taxed under reverse charge. The equalisation levy no longer applies. Guide: GST for foreign SaaS selling into India.

## How we work with clients abroad

- Fully remote: engagement letter and NDA by e-signature, data through your virtual data room or a shared drive, calls on your time zone (US mornings, Europe and Gulf afternoons, Japan and Singapore mornings IST).

- In English, in writing: every finding is referenced to a document or a public record, so your board, lawyers or auditors can rely on it.

- On the ground when needed: offices in Ahmedabad, Mumbai, Bengaluru, Rajkot and Dubai for site visits, bank meetings and management interviews.

- Clear scope: CA work — accounting, tax, FEMA and corporate filings. Legal opinions come from your lawyers; we work alongside them.
Related: tax notices and representation · paying Indian freelancers.

## Frequently asked questions
Why is my Indian customer deducting tax from my invoice?
Indian law requires payers to withhold tax on many payments to non-residents, such as royalties and fees for technical services. With a tax residency certificate, Form 41 and other documents, the lower rate in your country's treaty — or nil, for business profits without a permanent establishment — can usually be applied.

What replaced Form 10F in India?
From 1 April 2026, under the Income-tax Rules 2026, the treaty-relief information form is Form 41. It is filed online and supports the tax residency certificate.

Does a foreign company need a PAN in India?
It needs one to file an Indian return or apply for a lower-withholding certificate, and many Indian payers ask for one; without a PAN, withholding can be at a higher rate unless prescribed details are provided.

Does a foreign company have to file an income tax return in India?
Generally yes if it has income taxable in India. It is exempt only where its Indian income is limited to dividends, certain interest, royalties or technical fees and tax was withheld at not less than the domestic rates.

Tax representation

# An Indian tax notice, handled from start to finish

Notices from India’s income-tax or GST departments arrive by email and portal, often with short deadlines. We act as your authorised representative — reading the notice, gathering evidence, replying and seeing it through.

Send us the notice
hello@durgeshchavda.com

Talk it through first — free. Book a 15-minute intro call with Durgesh to scope your requirement, timeline and fee.Book a free 15-min intro

## Notices we handle

Notice about | Typical for | 

Mismatch between return and tax statements (TDS, high-value transactions) | NRIs, foreign companies with Indian income | 

Scrutiny / faceless assessment | Indian subsidiaries, foreign companies, NRIs | 

Reassessment of earlier years | Property sales, unreported foreign assets or income | 

Transfer-pricing questions | Subsidiaries of foreign groups | 

Withholding defaults on payments abroad | Indian companies paying foreign vendors | 

GST notices and audits | Indian entities, foreign SaaS suppliers registered under OIDAR | 

## How we handle them

- Read the notice and tell you, in plain English, what it’s really asking and the deadline.

- Collect and organise the evidence; reconcile figures with the department’s records.

- File replies online and attend virtual hearings as your authorised representative.

- If an order goes against you, appeal to the Commissioner (Appeals) and onward — coordinating with counsel where a matter needs a lawyer.

## Refunds of excess tax

Foreign companies and NRIs often have tax withheld at the wrong rate. We file the return, apply the treaty and follow the refund through. Related: India tax for foreign companies · NRI tax services.

## Frequently asked questions
Can a foreign company respond to an Indian tax notice without travelling to India?
Yes. Most income-tax and GST proceedings are online and faceless; a Chartered Accountant can act as your authorised representative, file replies and attend virtual hearings.

What should an NRI do on receiving an income tax notice in India?
Check the deadline and what is asked, gather the documents (TDS certificates, sale deeds, bank statements) and reply on the e-filing portal — or appoint a CA as authorised representative to handle it.

Can you claim an Indian tax refund for a foreign company?
Yes — by filing an Indian return that applies the treaty rate and following the refund through the portal.

US incorporation

# US company registration from India — Delaware C-Corp or LLC, done right on both sides

Most US formation services stop at the certificate. The expensive mistakes happen afterwards — on the Indian side and in year-one US compliance. We handle both.

Start your US company
hello@durgeshchavda.com

Talk it through first — free. Book a 15-minute intro call with Durgesh to scope your requirement, timeline and fee.Book a free 15-min intro
Free tool: Delaware franchise tax calculator — Both methods side by side — see why the Assumed Par Value Capital method usually wins.

## Why Indian founders incorporate in the US

- US investors and accelerators — many invest only in a Delaware C-Corp on standard documents.

- US customers — enterprise buyers often prefer contracting with a US entity and paying a US bank account.

- Payments and payouts — US payment processors, marketplaces and app stores are simpler with a US company.

- Hiring and equity — US-style stock options for US team members.

The part most founders miss: if you live in India, owning a US company is an overseas investment under FEMA. It has to be routed and reported correctly through your Indian bank, and it changes what you disclose in your Indian tax return. See FEMA, ODI & tax rules when Indians own a US company.

## What’s included

### US side

- Entity and state choice — C-Corp vs LLC, Delaware vs Wyoming vs your operating state. Compare C-Corp and LLC.

- Formation — Certificate of Incorporation / Formation, registered agent, bylaws or operating agreement, founder share issuance and board consents.

- EIN — IRS employer identification number, including for founders without an SSN or ITIN.

- Bank account support — document pack and guidance for opening a US business account remotely.

- Tax setup — elections, bookkeeping structure and the federal filings your entity type needs, including Form 5472 for foreign-owned LLCs.

- Annual compliance — Delaware annual report and franchise tax, federal returns and state registrations where you have operations.

### India side

- ODI structuring — whether founders invest personally under LRS or through an Indian company, within the Overseas Investment Rules, 2022.

- Form FC and bank documentation — reporting the investment through your AD bank, share-certificate submission and the annual APR.

- Income-tax reporting — Schedule FA disclosure, foreign tax credit and TCS on remittances.

- Transfer pricing — if an Indian company provides services to (or owns) the US entity.

- Parent–subsidiary set-up — for existing Indian companies, see US Delaware holdco structuring.

## How it works

01
### Structure
Entity, state, shareholding and the India-side route agreed before anything is filed.

02
### Form & register
US formation, EIN and bank documents; Indian ODI reporting as funds are remitted.

03
### Stay compliant
A single compliance calendar across Delaware, the IRS and India — tracked and filed.

## Cost of registering a US company from India

Item | Who sets it | Amount / note | 

State filing fee | The state | Wyoming LLC: $100. Delaware revised many filing fees from 1 August 2026 — check the current schedule | 

Registered agent | Private provider | Annual fee — compare renewal prices (how to choose) | 

EIN | IRS | Free | 

Delaware annual costs | Delaware | Corporations: $50 report + franchise tax (minimum $175 or $400 by method); LLCs: $400 a year from the 2026 tax year (first due 1 June 2027) | 

India side | Your bank / tax law | ODI reporting through your bank; 20% TCS on remittances above ₹10 lakh a year (creditable) | 

Full breakdown: what a US company really costs from India.

## Documents required

- Passport of each founder or member, and proof of address in India.

- PAN — needed for the overseas investment remittance from India.

- Proposed company name, business activity, shareholding and directors/managers.

- For the bank account: identity verification and a description of the business and expected transactions.

## How long it takes

- Formation — state filing can be completed within days.

- EIN — founders without an SSN apply by phone, fax or mail, which takes longer than the online route. See EIN without SSN.

- Bank account — once the EIN is issued. See US bank account from India.

- India-side ODI — remit and report through your bank; then the Annual Performance Report every 31 December.

## Year-one compliance calendar

What | Who | When | 

Delaware annual report + franchise tax | Delaware corporations | 1 March | 

Delaware annual LLC tax ($400 for the 2026 tax year onwards, first payable by 1 June 2027) | Delaware LLCs | 1 June | 

Form 1120 federal return | C-Corps (calendar year) | 15 April (extendable with Form 7004) | 

Pro forma Form 1120 + Form 5472 | Foreign-owned single-member LLCs | 15 April (extendable with Form 7004) | 

Form 1099-NEC | If you paid US contractors | 31 January | 

Annual Performance Report (APR) | Indian resident / entity with ODI | 31 December, every year | 

Schedule FA (foreign assets) in ITR | Indian resident shareholders | With the Indian income-tax return | 

Full month-by-month version: US company compliance calendar.

Missing these is where formation “savings” disappear: the Form 5472 penalty alone starts at $25,000.

## Frequently asked questions
Can an Indian resident register a company in the USA?
Yes. Non-US residents can form a US corporation or LLC in any state. If you live in India, investing in that company is an overseas investment under FEMA and must be made and reported through your Indian bank under the Overseas Investment Rules, 2022.

Which is better for Indian founders — Delaware C-Corp or LLC?
If you plan to raise venture capital or issue stock options, a Delaware C-Corp is usually the right choice. LLCs can suit simpler businesses, but create extra US filings for foreign owners and can be treated differently for Indian tax purposes.

Do I need to visit the US to incorporate?
No. Formation, EIN and in many cases bank account opening can be completed remotely.

How do I get an EIN without an SSN or ITIN?
Foreign founders without an SSN or ITIN apply for an EIN using IRS Form SS-4 — by phone on the IRS international line, by fax or by mail — rather than the online application.

Do US companies still need to file a BOI report with FinCEN?
No. Under FinCEN's final rule effective August 2026, entities formed in the United States are exempt from beneficial ownership (BOI) reporting. Only foreign companies registered to do business in a US state still report.

What ongoing compliance does a Delaware company have?
Delaware corporations file an annual report and pay franchise tax by 1 March; Delaware LLCs pay a flat annual tax by 1 June — $400 for the 2026 tax year onwards (first payable by 1 June 2027), up from $300 under Delaware HB 400. Federal returns (Form 1120, or pro forma 1120 with Form 5472 for foreign-owned LLCs) are generally due 15 April.

How much does it cost to register a company in the USA from India?
The state filing fee (for example $100 for a Wyoming LLC; Delaware revised its fees from 1 August 2026), a registered agent's annual fee and professional fees. The EIN is free. Ongoing costs include Delaware franchise tax or LLC tax, federal returns and India-side ODI reporting.

How long does it take to register a US company from India?
State formation can be done within days. The EIN takes longer for founders without an SSN because it is applied for by phone, fax or mail, and the bank account follows once the EIN is issued.

Can I open a US bank account for my company from India?
Usually yes — many US banks and fintech platforms open business accounts remotely once the company has its formation documents and EIN.

Do I need RBI approval to own a US company?
Not usually. Most investments by Indian residents into a US operating company fall under the automatic route of the Overseas Investment Rules, 2022 — but they must be made and reported through your authorised dealer bank (Form FC), with an Annual Performance Report every year.

India → US flip

# India to US flip — a Delaware parent without the FEMA and tax surprises

US investors often want a Delaware C-Corp. Getting there from an Indian company is where most mistakes happen: a share swap that FEMA doesn’t allow, a capital-gains bill nobody modelled, or a US parent that India treats as Indian. We design the route before anything is signed.

Plan your flip
hello@durgeshchavda.com

## When a flip makes sense

A Delaware parent helps when your lead investors require it, most revenue comes from US customers, founders are moving to the US, or a US acquisition is the likely exit. If your investors, customers and likely IPO are Indian, it often costs more than it’s worth — and reversing it later can cost far more. The full decision test is in our Delaware flip guide.

## The three routes

Route | How it works | Where it gets hard | 

Fresh US parent + migration | Incorporate the Delaware parent, raise into it, set up or move operations to a subsidiary and migrate the business over time | Slower; IP and contracts must move cleanly; transfer pricing from day one | 

Share swap | Shareholders of the Indian company exchange their shares for shares of the Delaware company, which then owns the Indian company | FEMA: resident individuals can acquire foreign shares by swap only in limited cases, and an individual who controls a foreign company can’t have it own subsidiaries — so a plain founder swap usually doesn’t work on the automatic route. Taxable for resident shareholders. | 

Indian entity holds the US stake | Founders invest via an Indian company or LLP, which makes the overseas direct investment under the more flexible entity rules | Adds a layer; round-tripping rules limit structures to two layers of subsidiaries | 

## The FEMA blocker most founders hit

Under the Overseas Investment Rules, 2022, a resident individual can make overseas direct investment only in an operating foreign company that isn’t in financial services — and if the individual has control (which can mean as little as 10% of voting rights through agreements), that company can’t have subsidiaries or step-down subsidiaries. A classic flip makes the Indian company a subsidiary of a founder-controlled Delaware parent, which is exactly the structure the rules restrict. Individuals can also acquire foreign shares by swap only in specified cases such as mergers. Holdings acquired in breach have to be unwound — so the route must be chosen first.

## Tax

- Share swap: for resident shareholders, exchanging Indian shares for Delaware shares is a taxable transfer — capital gains on the fair value received, with no general exemption.

- Losses: a change in ownership can cause the Indian company’s carried-forward losses to lapse — model it.

- POEM: if the Delaware company is in substance managed from India, India can treat it as an Indian tax resident.

- Transfer pricing: the Indian subsidiary must be paid at arm’s length — see India–US transfer pricing.

- US side: federal tax, Delaware franchise tax, Form 1120 and related reporting — see the compliance calendar.

## Filings checklist

- Overseas investment by Indian residents: Form FC through the authorised dealer bank when the investment is made; an Annual Performance Report by 31 December every year.

- Indian shares moving to the US parent: FC-TRS within 60 days of the transfer or receipt of consideration, whichever is earlier.

- New shares issued by the Indian company to the parent: FC-GPR within 30 days of allotment; then the annual FLA return.

- Valuations on both legs — FEMA pricing for the Indian shares and, for swaps, a valuation by a SEBI-registered merchant banker (or an overseas regulated investment banker) for the foreign shares.

- Investors from countries sharing a land border with India (e.g. a Chinese shareholder) need government approval.

## After the flip

- ESOPs: mirror or re-grant options over Delaware shares — see US parent ESOPs and 409A vs Indian valuation.

- Intercompany agreement, cost-plus billing and the annual transfer-pricing report.

- Delaware franchise tax on the right method — see the franchise tax guide.

- Investor-ready books on both sides — see the due diligence checklist.

## Delaware vs Singapore vs DIFC — a quick comparison

Jurisdiction | Typically chosen when | Watch-outs | 

US — Delaware | US VCs and accelerators, US customers and hiring, US exit | US tax on the parent, ODI and POEM planning for Indian founders | 

Singapore | Southeast Asian investors and markets | Resident-director rule, India–Singapore treaty conditions | 

UAE — DIFC / free zones | Middle East customers and investors | Qualifying-income conditions, POEM if run from India | 

USD 3.75MPre-Series A led and closed end-to-end for an AI EdTech startup
5+ yearsacross audit, tax, FEMA and startup finance
₹5,000 Cr+PSU bank audit portfolio handled early in career

## Frequently asked questions
What is a Delaware flip?
A Delaware flip puts a US (Delaware) parent company on top of an Indian startup, so founders and investors hold shares in the US company and the Indian company becomes its subsidiary — through a share swap, a fresh parent with migration, or an Indian entity holding the US stake.

Can Indian founders do a share swap into a Delaware company?
Usually not in its plain form on the automatic route. Under the Overseas Investment Rules, 2022, resident individuals can acquire foreign shares by swap only in specified cases, and a founder who controls a foreign company cannot have it own subsidiaries. The structure must be designed so that the FEMA route works.

Is a Delaware flip taxable in India?
For resident shareholders, swapping Indian shares for shares of the US company is generally a taxable transfer, with capital gains based on the fair value received; there is no general exemption.

What filings are needed for a flip?
Form FC and annual APRs for overseas investment by Indian residents, FC-TRS within 60 days when Indian shares move to the US parent, FC-GPR within 30 days for new shares issued to it, valuations on both legs, and the annual FLA return.

Can you also reverse a flip?
Yes — see the reverse flip service for moving a Delaware or Singapore holding company back to India.

US → India reverse flip

# Reverse flip to India — bring your holding company home

PhonePe, Groww, Razorpay, Meesho, Zepto and Flipkart have all moved their holding companies back to India, mostly ahead of Indian listings. The route you choose decides whether the move is close to tax-neutral or very expensive. We model it first.

Plan your reverse flip
hello@durgeshchavda.com

## Why companies flip back

- Indian IPOs: Groww, Pine Labs and Meesho listed in India within months of flipping back.

- Founder ESOPs: since June 2025, SEBI lets founders classified as promoters keep ESOPs granted at least a year before the draft prospectus.

- Simplicity: one main jurisdiction instead of two sets of compliance, transfer pricing and investor reporting.

## The routes

Route | Approvals | Tax in India | 

Inbound merger (NCLT) — the foreign holdco merges into the Indian company | NCLT scheme under the Companies Act with the cross-border merger rules; FEMA cross-border merger regulations | Can be tax-neutral when the amalgamation conditions are met (all assets and liabilities pass; holders of 75% in value become shareholders) | 

Fast-track merger — foreign holding company into its Indian subsidiary | Regional Director instead of NCLT (available since September 2024, widened in 2025); RBI approval — the 2026 FEMA amendment aligned the regulations, so confirm the current position with your bank | As above | 

Share swap — shareholders of the foreign holdco take Indian shares | FEMA swap rules (since August 2024); government approval for investors from land-border countries | Generally taxable — no specific exemption | 

## Tax: India and abroad

- India: the merger route can be tax-neutral for the company and its shareholders if the amalgamation conditions are met; swaps and purchases generally aren’t. Non-resident shareholders may also face Indian tax on indirect transfers.

- US (Delaware holdcos): moving the parent out of the US can trigger US corporate-level gain and the anti-inversion rules — unless the group has substantial business activities in India. This is usually the biggest cost; we work with your US tax counsel.

- Singapore holdcos: typically a smaller exit cost, but check the Singapore position on gains.

- Reported costs have been large — PhonePe’s shareholders reportedly paid about ₹8,000 crore — which is why the route matters.

## How we run it

01
### Feasibility & tax model
Cap table, investor mix, routes compared, Indian and foreign tax modelled with your US or Singapore advisers.

02
### Approvals
Valuations, scheme or swap documents with your lawyers, RBI and MCA/NCLT applications, investor consents.

03
### Close & clean up
FEMA filings, ESOP migration, cap table, wind-down of the foreign entity and IPO-readiness of the books.

Background reading: reverse flip guide · the original Delaware flip guide.

USD 3.75MPre-Series A led and closed end-to-end for an AI EdTech startup
5+ yearsacross audit, tax, FEMA and startup finance
₹5,000 Cr+PSU bank audit portfolio handled early in career

## Frequently asked questions
What is a reverse flip?
A reverse flip moves a startup's holding company from abroad — usually Delaware or Singapore — back to India, so that an Indian company sits at the top of the group, typically ahead of an Indian IPO.

Is a reverse flip taxable?
In India, an inbound merger can be tax-neutral if the amalgamation conditions are met, while share swaps are generally taxable. For a Delaware holding company, the US side — corporate-level gain and anti-inversion rules — is often the largest cost.

How long does a reverse flip take?
It depends on the route: an NCLT merger takes longer than the Regional Director fast-track route, and RBI, government or investor approvals can add time. Plan several months, and start with a tax model.

Which companies have done a reverse flip?
PhonePe, Groww, Zepto, Dream Sports, Razorpay, Meesho, Pine Labs and Flipkart have moved their holding companies to India, several ahead of Indian listings.

NRI tax & investments

# NRI tax, handled from India — so you don’t have to fly back for it

Selling a flat, moving money out, claiming a TDS refund or working out whether you’re still an NRI — we handle the Indian side remotely for NRIs in the UAE, US, UK, Canada, Australia, Singapore and the Gulf.

Ask about your NRI tax
hello@durgeshchavda.com

Quick answers

- Do NRIs have to pay tax in India? Yes — but only on Indian income: rent from Indian property, interest on NRO deposits, dividends, and capital gains on Indian shares, funds and property. Salary earned and paid abroad, and other foreign income, is not taxed in India.

- NRI tax slab 2026-27: the same slabs as residents (new regime: nil to ₹4 lakh, then 5% to 30%), but without the rebate that makes ₹12 lakh tax-free for residents.

- Interest on NRE and FCNR deposits is tax-free for NRIs; NRO interest is taxable.

- TDS: Indian payers deduct tax at source on most NRI income, often more than the final tax — file a return to get the excess back.

- Deemed resident: an Indian citizen with Indian income above ₹15 lakh who isn’t taxable in any other country can be treated as resident (RNOR) — check with the residential status calculator.

Free tools: capital gains & NRI TDS calculator · residential status calculator

New to NRI tax? Start with the complete NRI taxation guide.

## What we handle

- Income tax returns for NRIs — rent, interest, capital gains and TDS refunds. See NRI income tax return.

- Property sales — capital gains computation, a lower-TDS certificate before the sale, exemptions by reinvesting, and guidance for the buyer on deducting and depositing TDS.

- Repatriation — the CA certificate in Form 146, Form 145 filing and the documents your bank needs.

- Treaty relief — tax residency certificate, Form 41 (formerly 10F) and claiming the lower treaty rate.

- Residential status planning — for NRIs visiting often or returning to India (RNOR).

- Investing in India — Indian startups, AIFs and GIFT City funds.

## Selling property in India

When an NRI sells, the buyer must deduct TDS on the capital gain — on long-term gains at 12.5% plus surcharge and cess, which can take the effective rate to about 14.95%. From 1 October 2026, individual buyers no longer need a TAN to do this. A lower-TDS certificate, obtained before the sale, stops tax being over-deducted on the full sale price. Full guide: TDS on sale of property by an NRI.

## Moving money out

NRIs can remit up to USD 1 million per financial year from NRO balances and sale proceeds, with Form 145 and, for larger taxable amounts, a CA certificate in Form 146. See repatriating money from India.

## Are you still an NRI?

Your status for the year depends on days in India — and, if your Indian income exceeds ₹15 lakh, the 60-day threshold becomes 120 days. Returning NRIs can often be RNOR for a period, which keeps foreign income out of Indian tax. See residential status and RNOR.

01
### Send the basics
PAN, passport travel dates, bank statements and details of the property or income — on WhatsApp or email.

02
### We compute & file
Tax computation, certificates and filings, with your approval before anything is submitted.

03
### Done remotely
No trip to India needed. Calls in your time zone — we have an office in Dubai.

Living in the UK? NRIs in the UK: Indian tax and UK tax.
Living in Canada? NRIs in Canada: Indian tax and Canadian tax.

## Frequently asked questions
Do NRIs have to file an income tax return in India?
An NRI must file if Indian taxable income exceeds the basic exemption limit, and should file to claim a refund of excess TDS — common after a property sale or on NRO interest.

How much TDS is deducted when an NRI sells property in India?
On long-term capital gains, TDS is 12.5% plus surcharge (up to 15%) and 4% cess, an effective rate of up to about 14.95%. Short-term gains are taxed at slab rates, so TDS is typically 30% plus surcharge and cess. A lower-TDS certificate can reduce this.

How much money can an NRI repatriate from India?
Up to USD 1 million per financial year from NRO balances, sale proceeds of assets and inheritance, with Form 145 and, where required, a CA certificate in Form 146.

Can you help without me travelling to India?
Yes. Returns, lower-TDS certificate applications, CA certificates and treaty-relief forms are handled online. Durgesh works with NRIs across the UAE, US, UK, Canada, Australia, Singapore and the Gulf.

GIFT City · IFSC

# Set up in GIFT City — funds, family offices and companies, handled end to end

GIFT City’s International Financial Services Centre (IFSC) is India’s offshore financial hub, with a 20-year tax holiday and dollar-denominated operations. Our Ahmedabad office is half an hour away.

Discuss a GIFT City setup
hello@durgeshchavda.com

Talk it through first — free. Book a 15-minute intro call with Durgesh to scope your requirement, timeline and fee.Book a free 15-min intro

## What GIFT IFSC is

GIFT City in Gandhinagar, Gujarat, hosts India’s International Financial Services Centre, regulated by a single regulator — the International Financial Services Centres Authority (IFSCA). A unit in the IFSC is treated as a person resident outside India for foreign-exchange purposes, operates in foreign currency, and gets tax incentives that the rest of India doesn’t.

It has grown quickly: by 30 June 2026 there were about 235 fund management entities running some 400 schemes, according to IFSCA data reported by Cafemutual.

## What you can set up

- Fund management entity (FME) and funds — venture capital schemes, restricted schemes equivalent to Category I, II and III AIFs, retail schemes and ETFs. See how to set up a fund in GIFT City.

- Family office — a single-family Family Investment Fund (minimum USD 10 million within three years) or a multi-family office under a portfolio-management licence. See family office in India or GIFT City.

- Book-keeping, accounting, tax and financial-crime compliance (BATF) services for non-resident clients, under IFSCA’s 2024 regulations.

- Global in-house centres for financial-institution groups, under regulations effective December 2025.

- Other regulated activities — banking units, insurance, capital-market intermediaries, aircraft and ship leasing, fintech and bullion — each with its own IFSCA framework.

FME category | Minimum net worth | What it can manage | 

Authorised FME | USD 75,000 | Venture Capital Schemes; single-family Family Investment Funds | 

Registered FME (Non-Retail) | USD 500,000 | Restricted schemes (Category I, II and III AIF equivalents), portfolio management including multi-family offices, private REITs/InvITs | 

Registered FME (Retail) | USD 1,000,000 | Retail schemes, ETFs and public REITs/InvITs — with board independence and track-record conditions | 

Source: IFSCA (Fund Management) Regulations, 2025, as amended. Managing third-party funds adds USD 500,000 to the net-worth requirement.

## Why the numbers work

- Tax holiday: after the Finance Act 2026, eligible IFSC units get a 100% deduction of business income for 20 consecutive years out of 25, and a concessional 15% rate after that.

- Non-resident investors: a range of exemptions for income from specified IFSC funds and securities traded on IFSC exchanges.

- Fund relocation: tax-neutral moves of eligible offshore funds to GIFT City, available until 31 March 2030.

- GST: services received by IFSC units are broadly outside GST.

Details and conditions: GIFT City tax benefits.

## How setup works

- Structure — activity, licence category, legal form (company, LLP or branch), capital and people.

- Incorporate the entity and set up the IFSC office.

- Apply through the Single Window IT System (SWIT) — one application covers the IFSCA licence or registration and the SEZ approval.

- Substance — key managerial persons based in the IFSC, bank account with an IFSC banking unit, policies and compliance manual.

- Launch — for funds, file the placement memorandum; venture capital and restricted schemes can open once IFSCA takes it on record (“green channel”).

## How we help

- Feasibility: GIFT City vs a SEBI AIF vs an offshore fund — see VC fund setup.

- Entity setup, IFSCA and SEZ applications, bank accounts and the capital inflow.

- Fund accounting, NAV support, tax filings, transfer pricing and IFSCA reporting after launch.

- Investor-side advice for resident Indians (LRS) and NRIs — see how to invest in GIFT City.

## Frequently asked questions
What is GIFT IFSC?
GIFT IFSC is India's International Financial Services Centre in GIFT City, Gandhinagar, Gujarat. It is regulated by the IFSCA, units there are treated as non-residents for foreign-exchange purposes, and they receive tax incentives including a 20-year tax holiday.

What are the tax benefits of setting up in GIFT City?
After the Finance Act 2026, eligible IFSC units can claim a 100% deduction of business income for any 20 consecutive years out of 25, followed by a concessional 15% rate. There are also exemptions for non-resident investors in specified funds and securities, tax-neutral fund relocation until 31 March 2030, and GST relief on services received.

How much net worth does a fund management entity in GIFT City need?
Under the IFSCA (Fund Management) Regulations, 2025: USD 75,000 for an Authorised FME, USD 500,000 for a Registered FME (Non-Retail) and USD 1,000,000 for a Registered FME (Retail), with an extra USD 500,000 for third-party fund management.

Can Indian residents invest in GIFT City?
Yes. Since July 2024 RBI allows remittances under the Liberalised Remittance Scheme (up to USD 250,000 a financial year) to IFSCs for all permissible purposes, including IFSCA-regulated financial products.

How far is your office from GIFT City?
About 30 minutes. Durgesh's office is in Ahmedabad, next to Gandhinagar, and he also has an office in Dubai for UAE-based clients.

VC / AIF funds

# Starting a venture capital fund? SEBI AIF or GIFT City — structured and launched right

Emerging managers, angel networks, family offices and corporates use us to pick the vehicle, get registered, reach first close and run the fund’s finance and compliance.

Plan your fund
hello@durgeshchavda.com

## Choose the vehicle

| SEBI AIF (India) | GIFT City scheme (IFSC) | 

Currency | Indian rupees | US dollars (or other foreign currency) | 

Minimum corpus | ₹20 crore per scheme | USD 3 million (venture capital and restricted schemes) | 

Minimum per investor | ₹1 crore (₹25 lakh for employees); none for accredited investors | USD 250,000 (VC scheme) or USD 150,000 (restricted scheme) | 

Best fit | Mostly Indian investors backing Indian companies | Global, NRI and foreign investors; India and overseas investments | 

Full comparison: GIFT City fund vs SEBI AIF.

## SEBI AIF in brief

- Category I covers venture capital, angel, SME, social impact and infrastructure funds; Category II is private equity and debt; Category III runs trading strategies. See AIF categories explained.

- Apply online on SEBI’s intermediary portal. The team needs at least one NISM-certified person and one with a relevant professional qualification.

- Since July 2026 a scheme can launch 10 working days after filing its placement memorandum through a merchant banker, and the scheme fee for the first scheme is waived.

- Category I and II AIFs are tax pass-through for most income. See AIF taxation.

Step-by-step: SEBI AIF registration process. Running an angel network? See angel funds under SEBI’s new rules.

## GIFT City in brief

- Register a fund management entity with IFSCA — an Authorised FME (USD 75,000 net worth) can run venture capital schemes.

- Venture capital and restricted schemes open as soon as IFSCA takes the placement memorandum on record.

- IFSC tax holiday of 20 years out of 25 for the manager, and exemptions for non-resident investors.

More: how to set up a fund in GIFT City.

## What we do

01
### Structure
Vehicle, category, sponsor and manager entities, economics (fees, carry, hurdle), tax model for investors.

02
### Register & launch
SEBI or IFSCA application, team eligibility, placement memorandum inputs, bank and custodian, first close.

03
### Run the fund
Fund accounting, capital calls and distributions, valuations, SEBI/IFSCA reporting, tax and investor statements.

Durgesh has sat on the other side of the table: as Finance Head of Stimuler he led a USD 3.75M Pre-Series A end-to-end, so he knows what portfolio reporting founders can realistically deliver.

## Frequently asked questions
How do I start a venture capital fund in India?
Choose between a SEBI-registered Category I AIF (venture capital sub-category) in rupees or a GIFT City venture capital scheme in dollars; set up the sponsor, manager and fund vehicle; register with SEBI or IFSCA; file the placement memorandum; and declare first close within 12 months.

What is the minimum corpus for an AIF in India?
₹20 crore per scheme for SEBI AIFs. Social impact funds need ₹5 crore. A GIFT City venture capital or restricted scheme needs at least USD 3 million.

How long does it take to launch a SEBI AIF?
After registration, a scheme can launch 10 working days after its placement memorandum is filed through a merchant banker, under the process introduced in July 2026. Registration time itself depends on SEBI's review.

Should I set up my fund in GIFT City or as a SEBI AIF?
If most investors are Indian residents investing in rupees into Indian companies, a SEBI AIF is usually simpler. If investors are global or NRIs, or the fund invests outside India, a GIFT City scheme is often a better fit.

## What a Virtual CFO does for you

Most early-stage companies have bookkeeping and a tax consultant. What they don’t have is someone who turns those numbers into decisions — how much runway you really have, which channel is actually profitable, and what investors will ask in the next board meeting. That is the job of a Virtual CFO.

- 3-statement financial models — P&L, balance sheet and cash flow, linked and scenario-ready.

- Monthly MIS and board packs — a consistent monthly close with an investor update deck your board can read in ten minutes.

- Runway and burn monitoring — cash forecasts that flag problems months before they become emergencies.

FEMA & RBI

# FEMA & RBI compliance that keeps up with your growth

One missed FC-GPR or delayed RBI filing can hold up your next round. Every foreign-investment filing — reported correctly and on time.

Get your filings sorted
hello@durgeshchavda.com

Talk it through first — free. Book a 15-minute intro call with Durgesh to scope your requirement, timeline and fee.Book a free 15-min intro
Free tool: FEMA late submission fee calculator — LSF for late FC-GPR, FC-TRS, ODI and other filings under RBI's formula.

## Filings we handle

- FC-GPR — reporting the issue of shares or convertible instruments to foreign investors. Read the FC-GPR guide.

- FC-TRS — reporting transfers of shares between residents and non-residents. Read the FC-TRS guide.

- ODI filings — overseas direct investment into foreign subsidiaries or holding companies under the Overseas Investment Rules, 2022.

- Annual FLA return — the Foreign Liabilities and Assets return for companies with FDI or ODI.

- Valuation and pricing — fair-value certificates that satisfy FEMA pricing guidelines.

- RBI approvals and regularisation — approval-route cases, late-submission fees and compounding where something was missed.

- Companies Act, ROC and LLP compliance, and NBFC regulatory frameworks.

## Key deadlines at a glance

Event | Filing | Timeline | 

Shares / convertibles issued to a non-resident | FC-GPR (FIRMS portal) | Within 30 days of allotment | 

Transfer of shares between resident and non-resident | FC-TRS (FIRMS portal) | Within 60 days of transfer or receipt/remittance of funds, whichever is earlier | 

Company holds FDI and/or ODI | FLA return | Annually, by 15 July | 

Investment into a foreign entity | ODI forms via AD bank | As prescribed under the OI Rules/Regulations, 2022 | 

## Why it matters

FEMA reporting sits at the intersection of your AD bank, the RBI’s FIRMS portal, your company secretary and your valuer. Delays usually come from small mismatches — a FIRC that doesn’t match the allotment, a valuation dated after the issue, or a missing KYC. Late filings can be regularised by paying a late-submission fee, but repeated or long delays may need compounding and will be flagged in future due diligence.

Durgesh has handled FC-GPR reporting and ODI filings for venture-backed companies, including around a USD 3.75M Pre-Series A, and advises on cross-border structures through US Delaware, Singapore, DIFC and Mauritius holding companies.
Foreign company with an Indian subsidiary or Indian customers? See Indian subsidiary compliance and India tax for foreign companies.
Coming change: draft FEMA Foreign Investment Rules 2026.
Selling or raising from abroad? Vendor (sell-side) due diligence in India.

## Frequently asked questions
What is the deadline for filing FC-GPR?
FC-GPR must be filed on the RBI's FIRMS portal within 30 days from the date of allotment of shares or other capital instruments to a person resident outside India.

Who files FC-TRS — the buyer or the seller?
Generally the resident party to the transfer (buyer or seller) is responsible for filing FC-TRS, within 60 days of the transfer or of receipt/remittance of funds, whichever is earlier.

What happens if an FEMA filing is delayed?
Delayed reporting can usually be regularised by paying a Late Submission Fee (LSF) calculated on the amount involved and the period of delay, within the time window the RBI allows. Beyond that, compounding may be required.

Do startups with foreign investors need to file the FLA return?
Yes. Indian companies that have received FDI and/or made overseas direct investment must file the annual Foreign Liabilities and Assets (FLA) return by 15 July each year.

Overseas incorporation

# Setting up a company abroad from India — US, Singapore, UAE or UK

Incorporating abroad takes days. Getting the Indian side right — overseas direct investment rules, bank reporting, tax disclosures and where the company is really managed from — is what protects you later. We do both.

Plan your overseas company
hello@durgeshchavda.com

## Choosing a country

| United States | Singapore | UAE | United Kingdom | 

Best for | US investors, customers, SaaS | Asia HQ, investors in SE Asia | Middle East customers, Gulf capital | UK and European customers | 

Local director needed? | No | Yes — one ordinarily resident director | Depends on licence; no Emirati shareholder needed for most activities | No (UK registered office needed) | 

Corporate tax | 21% federal plus state | 17%, with start-up and partial exemptions | 0% up to AED 375,000, then 9% (0% on qualifying free zone income) | 19% to 25% | 

Guide | US incorporation | Singapore | Dubai / UAE | UK | 

## The India side: overseas direct investment (ODI)

Any investment by an Indian resident into the shares of an unlisted foreign company is ODI under FEMA’s Overseas Investment Rules, 2022 — whether it’s USD 1 or USD 1 million.

| Resident individual (founder) | Indian company | 

Route | ODI within the Liberalised Remittance Scheme | ODI under the automatic route | 

Limit | USD 250,000 per financial year (all LRS remittances together) | Up to 400% of net worth; RBI approval above USD 1 billion in a year | 

What you can invest in | Only an operating foreign company, not in financial services, and — if you control it — one with no subsidiaries of its own | Operating companies and, with conditions, holding structures | 

Reporting | Form FC through your bank; Annual Performance Report by 31 December | Form FC; Annual Performance Report by 31 December | 

Tax side | 20% TCS on remittances above ₹10 lakh a year (creditable); disclose in Schedule FA | Transfer pricing on dealings with the subsidiary | 

Late filings can usually be regularised with a late submission fee within three years — but until then you can’t make further investments. Details: ODI rules for founders.

## Where the company is managed from

If the key management and commercial decisions of your foreign company are actually made in India, India can treat it as an Indian tax resident (“place of effective management”). Under the CBDT’s circular this applies to foreign companies with turnover above ₹50 crore, and treaty tie-breakers look at the same question. Plan board meetings, signatories and decision-making accordingly.

## How we do it

01
### Structure
Country, entity type, who holds the shares (you or your Indian company), tax model and an ODI plan.

02
### Incorporate & fund
Formation with local partners, bank account, and the remittance with Form FC through your bank.

03
### Stay compliant
Annual Performance Report, Schedule FA, transfer pricing and the foreign company’s own filings.

Already have a company abroad and want to bring it home? See the reverse flip service.

## Frequently asked questions
Can an Indian resident set up a company abroad?
Yes. A resident individual can invest in an operating foreign company under the overseas direct investment rules within the USD 250,000 annual LRS limit, and an Indian company can invest up to 400% of its net worth under the automatic route, with reporting through an authorised dealer bank.

What filings are needed after investing in a foreign company?
Form FC through your bank when the investment is made, and an Annual Performance Report by 31 December every year; resident individuals also disclose the shares in Schedule FA of their income-tax return.

Can an individual's foreign company have subsidiaries?
If the resident individual has control of the foreign company, it cannot have subsidiaries or step-down subsidiaries under the Overseas Investment Rules, 2022. An Indian company has more flexibility.

Which country is best for an Indian startup's overseas company?
It depends on investors and customers: the US (Delaware) for US VC and SaaS customers, Singapore for Southeast Asian investors and an Asia base, the UAE for Gulf markets and capital, and the UK for UK and European customers.

Foreign company guide

# Doing business in India: the 2026 guide for foreign companies

Singapore and the US were India’s two largest sources of foreign direct investment in 2025-26. Here’s how foreign companies enter, how they’re taxed and what they must file — updated for the new Income-tax Act and the 2026 FDI changes.

By CA Durgesh Chavda·Last reviewed 14 October 2026·7 min read

Plan your India entry
hello@durgeshchavda.com

Key takeaways
- Most sectors allow 100% foreign ownership under the automatic route; only reporting to RBI is needed.
- Since Press Note 2 (2026 Series), land-border-country investors with non-controlling beneficial ownership of up to 10% can use the automatic route.
- An Indian subsidiary can opt for a 22% base tax rate (about 25.17% all-in); a branch pays 35% plus surcharge and cess.

## Five ways to enter India

Option | Can earn revenue? | Best for | 

Employer of record | No (you contract from abroad) | First 1–10 hires while you test the market | 

Liaison office | No | Representation and market research only | 

Branch / project office | Yes, within permitted activities | Same legal entity as the parent; specific contracts | 

Private limited subsidiary | Yes | Most foreign companies — sales, engineering, GCCs | 

LLP | Yes | Services in sectors open to 100% automatic-route FDI | 

Not sure? Try the India entry structure chooser or read liaison, branch or project office.

## Foreign investment rules

- Most sectors allow 100% FDI under the automatic route — no prior approval, just reporting (FC-GPR within 30 days of issuing shares).

- Some sectors have caps or need government approval.

- Land-border countries (including China): since Press Note 2 (2026 Series), investors with non-controlling beneficial ownership of up to 10% can use the automatic route; above that, or with control, government approval is still needed.

## Tax in brief

- India’s Income-tax Act, 2025 applies from 1 April 2026; the tax year runs April–March.

- Subsidiary: 22% base rate option (about 25.17% all-in). Branch: 35% plus surcharge and cess.

- Payments abroad (dividends, royalties, technical fees, interest) carry withholding, reduced by treaties — see repatriating profits.

- Transfer pricing applies to every intercompany charge; GST at 18% on most services, with exports zero-rated.

## Hiring

India’s four Labour Codes have applied since 21 November 2025. Payroll includes provident fund, gratuity and professional tax; contractors who work like employees create both labour and permanent establishment risk.

## Annual compliance

Audit, AGM, MCA filings, income-tax and transfer-pricing returns, the FLA return to RBI by 15 July, and monthly GST, TDS and payroll filings. What that looks like in practice: Indian subsidiary compliance.

## Checking partners and targets

India’s public registries are unusually open — private companies’ accounts are on file with the government. Start with how to verify an Indian company; for investments use a due diligence checklist.

## Sources

- Business Standard — DPIIT amends Press Note 3 (Mar 2026)
- RBI Master Direction — establishment of branch, liaison or project offices

## Frequently asked questions
Can a foreign company own 100% of an Indian company?
Yes, in most sectors under the automatic route, with no prior approval — only post-investment reporting to RBI. Some sectors have caps or need government approval, as do investors with more than 10% beneficial ownership (or control) from countries sharing a land border with India.

What is the easiest way for a foreign company to start in India?
Many start with an employer of record for the first few hires, then set up a private limited subsidiary once the team or revenue grows. A liaison office suits companies that only need representation and market research.

How is a foreign company taxed in India?
An Indian subsidiary is taxed as an Indian company (22% base rate option, about 25.17% all-in). A branch is taxed at 35% plus surcharge and cess. Payments to the foreign parent carry withholding tax reduced by treaties.

How long does it take to set up a company in India?
Incorporation itself typically takes a few weeks once documents are apostilled or notarised; opening the bank account, bringing in capital and filing FC-GPR follow. Plan for one to two months end to end.

Supplier checks

# How to verify an Indian company before you sign or pay

Importers, buyers and investors abroad all need the same answer: is this Indian company real, and can it deliver? Most of the answer is in free government databases — if you know where to look.

By CA Durgesh Chavda·Last reviewed 14 October 2026·6 min read

Get a company checked
hello@durgeshchavda.com

Key takeaways
- MCA company master data, the GST taxpayer search and DGFT's IEC lookup are free.
- A company's filed financial statements can be viewed on MCA for about ₹100.
- The biggest red flag is a gap between what a supplier claims and what it has filed with the government.

## Free checks anyone can run

Check | Where | What it tells you | 

Company master data | MCA portal → “View Company/LLP Master Data” (free) | Legal name, CIN, incorporation date, status (active / struck off), registered address, paid-up capital, directors, last filing dates | 

Charges | MCA → “Index of Charges” (free) | Loans secured on the company’s assets, and which banks hold them | 

GST registration | GST portal → “Search Taxpayer” (free) | Whether the GSTIN is active, legal and trade name, place of business and whether returns are being filed | 

Import–export code | DGFT → “View any IEC” (free) | Whether the company is registered to import or export | 

Directors | MCA master data → each director’s DIN | Other companies they run — including struck-off ones | 

## The ₹100 check most people miss

For about ₹100 per company (₹50 for an LLP), MCA’s “View Public Documents” lets you read the company’s filed financial statements and annual returns — revenue, profit, debt, shareholders. A supplier claiming ₹100 crore of sales that files ₹2 crore with the government has told you what you need to know.

## Red flags

- Status “strike off”, “dormant” or “under process of striking off”; annual filings years behind.

- Bank details in a name different from the legal name, or a personal account.

- GSTIN cancelled or returns not filed for months.

- Paid-up capital of ₹1 lakh behind a claimed multi-crore operation.

- Directors linked to many struck-off companies.

- Pressure to pay an “advance” to a different entity “for tax reasons”.

## When to go deeper

For larger contracts, distributorships, JVs or investments, a CA can read the filed accounts properly, reconcile them with GST returns, check tax demands and court records, and interview management. That’s what due diligence in India covers — remotely, in English.

## Sources

- GST portal — Search Taxpayer user manual
- Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA21)
- DGFT — Directorate General of Foreign Trade
Partnering rather than investing? Due diligence on an Indian business partner (JV, distributor, supplier, licensee) · joint venture in India guide.
Want it done for you? India Company Check.
See also: reading the accounts: red flags.
See also: checking credit ratings and defaults.
Start small: an India Company Check on one Indian company — USD 249, report in 5 working days.

## Frequently asked questions
How can I check if an Indian company is legit?
Search its name or CIN on the MCA portal's free master data to confirm it exists and is active, check its GSTIN on the GST portal, and for about ₹100 view its filed financial statements on MCA. Mismatches between claims and filings are the main red flag.

Is MCA company search free?
Company and LLP master data and the index of charges are free to view. Viewing a company's filed documents, such as financial statements, costs about ₹100 per company (₹50 per LLP).

How do I check a GST number in India?
Use 'Search Taxpayer' on the GST portal without logging in. It shows whether the GSTIN is active, the legal and trade name, the principal place of business and the return-filing record.

Can I see the financial statements of a private company in India?
Yes. Indian private companies file financial statements with the Ministry of Corporate Affairs, and anyone can view them through MCA's public documents service for a small fee.

Investor checklist

# Due diligence checklist for Indian companies

The checklist we use when a foreign fund or company invests in, or buys, an Indian business — and why each line matters.

By CA Durgesh Chavda·Last reviewed 14 October 2026·6 min read

Get support on a deal
hello@durgeshchavda.com

Key takeaways
- Check every past foreign investment: FC-GPR within 30 days of allotment and FC-TRS within 60 days.
- Reconcile GST returns with the books and input credit with supplier filings.
- Pull open income-tax demands and TDS defaults from the government portals — they transfer with the company.

## Financial

- Audited financial statements for three years, with the latest management accounts and the trial balance.

- Revenue by customer, product and month; top-10 customer contracts; receivables ageing.

- Bank statements reconciled to the books — especially for cash-heavy businesses.

- Related-party transactions and balances; loans to and from promoters.

- Debt, guarantees and charges (cross-check MCA’s index of charges).

## Income tax and GST

- Income-tax returns, assessment orders and every open demand or notice on the e-filing portal.

- TDS returns and default notices — unpaid TDS becomes the buyer’s problem.

- GST: sales in returns vs books, input credit claimed vs credit available, export refunds and LUTs.

- Transfer-pricing reports if the company deals with group entities.

## FEMA and foreign investment

- Every share issue to non-residents: FC-GPR filed within 30 days, with a valuation certificate supporting the price.

- Every transfer between residents and non-residents: FC-TRS within 60 days of the transfer or receipt of funds, whichever is earlier, at a price within the pricing guidelines.

- FLA returns, ODI filings for overseas subsidiaries, ECB reporting.

- Sectoral caps and the beneficial-ownership position under Press Note 3 (as amended in 2026). Late filings can usually be fixed — at a cost; see the FEMA late fee calculator.

## Corporate and cap table

- Share-capital history from incorporation, reconciled to MCA filings and the register of members.

- ESOP scheme, grants and the pool; convertible notes and SAFEs — see the cap table guide.

- Board and shareholder approvals for key transactions; director KYC; statutory registers.

## Labour and payroll

- PF, ESI and professional tax registrations and payments; gratuity provisioning.

- Consultants who are really employees; key-person agreements and non-competes.

## Contracts, IP and licences

- Change-of-control clauses in customer, supplier and lease agreements.

- Trademark and IP ownership — in the company’s name, not the founder’s.

- Business licences and sector registrations (these, with litigation, are for your legal counsel).

Want it run for you? Due diligence in India — financial, tax and FEMA, with SPA drafting points.

## Sources

- Treelife — FC-TRS filing
- Income-tax e-filing portal
Partnering rather than investing? Due diligence on an Indian business partner (JV, distributor, supplier, licensee) · joint venture in India guide.
See also: 13 financial red flags.
See also: how much it costs.

## Frequently asked questions
What documents are needed for due diligence of an Indian company?
Typically three years of audited accounts, management accounts, bank statements, tax returns and assessments, GST returns, FEMA filings for foreign investment, the share-capital history, statutory registers, key contracts and payroll records.

What are the biggest red flags in Indian due diligence?
Unreported or mispriced foreign investment, GST input credit that doesn't match supplier filings, open tax demands, undisclosed charges on assets, cash or related-party transactions, and staff classed as consultants to avoid payroll taxes.

Who does FEMA due diligence in India?
Chartered Accountants experienced in RBI and FDI filings typically check FC-GPR, FC-TRS, pricing and FLA compliance, alongside legal counsel for sector and approval questions.

Please note: this guide is general information based on the rules as they stood on the review date above. Regulations and RBI/CBDT procedures change often — please get advice on your specific facts before acting.

M&A guide

# Acquiring a company in India as a foreign buyer

Share purchase, fresh issue or asset deal — each route has its own FEMA, tax and approval steps. Here’s the sequence foreign acquirers follow.

By CA Durgesh Chavda·Last reviewed 14 October 2026·6 min read

Discuss an acquisition
hello@durgeshchavda.com

Key takeaways
- Unlisted shares bought from a resident must be priced at or above fair value under FEMA.
- FC-TRS is due within 60 days of the transfer or receipt of funds, whichever is earlier.
- Buying from a non-resident seller means withholding tax under section 393(2) of the Income-tax Act, 2025.

## 1. Check the route

- Most sectors: automatic route — no prior approval.

- Capped or approval sectors: government approval before closing.

- Buyers with beneficial owners in a land-border country: under Press Note 2 (2026 Series), non-controlling beneficial ownership up to 10% can use the automatic route; more than that, or control, needs approval.

## 2. Price within the FEMA pricing guidelines

- Buying from a resident seller: price not less than fair value.

- A non-resident selling to a resident: price not more than fair value.

- Fair value of unlisted shares is set by an internationally accepted pricing method on an arm’s-length basis, certified by a CA, a SEBI-registered merchant banker or a practising cost accountant. Deferred or escrowed consideration is allowed within limits.

## 3. Report the transfer

FC-TRS on RBI’s FIRMS portal within 60 days of the transfer or receipt / remittance of funds, whichever is earlier — filed by the resident party. A fresh issue of shares instead needs FC-GPR within 30 days.

## 4. Tax on the deal

- The seller is taxed on capital gains. If you buy from a non-resident seller, you must withhold tax under section 393(2) of the Income-tax Act, 2025 — get a CA’s computation or a lower-withholding certificate.

- Buying from a resident below fair market value can create taxable income for the buyer; price support matters for tax as well as FEMA.

- Stamp duty on the share transfer and any carried-forward losses (which can lapse on a change in shareholding) also need checking.

## 5. Other approvals

- Competition Commission notification for larger deals, including the deal-value test.

- Listed targets: SEBI takeover rules — crossing 25% triggers an open offer.

- Sector regulators (banking, insurance, telecom) where relevant.

## Before all of this: diligence

Most post-deal surprises in India are unreported FDI, GST mismatches and tax demands — see the due diligence checklist and our due diligence service.

## Sources

- Vinod Kothari — Press Note 3 relaxation (Mar 2026)
- Treelife — FC-TRS filing
See also: financial red flags.
Coming change: draft Foreign Investment Rules 2026.
Selling or raising from abroad? Vendor (sell-side) due diligence in India.

## Frequently asked questions
Can a foreign company buy an Indian company?
Yes. In most sectors a foreign company can acquire up to 100% under the automatic route, subject to FEMA pricing guidelines and reporting the transfer in Form FC-TRS. Some sectors and land-border-country investors need government approval.

What is FC-TRS and when is it filed?
FC-TRS reports a transfer of shares between a resident and a non-resident. It is filed on RBI's FIRMS portal within 60 days of the transfer or receipt/remittance of funds, whichever is earlier, by the resident party.

Does the buyer have to deduct tax when buying shares in India?
When the seller is a non-resident, yes — the buyer must withhold tax on the capital gains under section 393(2) of the Income-tax Act, 2025, unless a lower or nil withholding certificate applies.

Please note: this guide is general information based on the rules as they stood on the review date above. Regulations and RBI/CBDT procedures change often — please get advice on your specific facts before acting.

Foreign company guide

# Liaison, branch or project office in India

Foreign companies can be present in India without forming an Indian company — but RBI decides what each type of office may do. Here are the current rules and what they cost you each year.

By CA Durgesh Chavda·Last reviewed 22 October 2026·6 min read

Plan your India office
hello@durgeshchavda.com

Key takeaways
- A liaison office needs 3 years of profits and USD 50,000 net worth; a branch 5 years and USD 100,000.
- A liaison office cannot earn income; it is generally valid for 3 years.
- From tax year 2026-27 the liaison office statement is Form 162 (formerly Form 49C).

## What is a liaison office in India?

A liaison office is a representative office a foreign company opens in India with permission processed by its bank under RBI rules. It can only act as a communication channel — representing the parent, promoting its products and collaboration — and cannot earn income or do business. A branch office, by contrast, can carry on permitted commercial activities and is taxed as a foreign company.

## At a glance

| Liaison office | Branch office | Project office | 

Purpose | Communication channel only | Permitted commercial activities | One specific project in India | 

Can earn income? | No | Yes | Yes, from the project | 

Track record | Profits in the last 3 years; net worth USD 50,000+ | Profits in the last 5 years; net worth USD 100,000+ | A contract from an Indian company | 

Validity | Usually 3 years, extendable | No fixed term | Life of the project | 

Taxed? | No income, but annual statement | As a foreign company (35% + surcharge, cess) | As a foreign company on project profit | 

A company that doesn’t meet the track record can apply with a letter of comfort from its parent.

## What a liaison office can — and can’t — do

- Can: represent the parent, promote exports and imports, promote technical or financial collaboration, and act as a communication channel.

- Can’t: trade, sign contracts as a business, earn any income or borrow. Its costs are met from the head office’s remittances.

- Validity is generally three years (two for NBFCs and construction companies); the bank can extend it if annual activity certificates are up to date.

## When you need prior RBI approval

- Applicants from Pakistan — always.

- Applicants from Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, Afghanistan, Iran, China, Hong Kong or Macau — for offices in Jammu & Kashmir, the North-East or Andaman & Nicobar.

- Defence, telecom, private security and information & broadcasting businesses; NGOs and foreign government bodies.

- Sectors not open to 100% FDI under the automatic route go through the government.

- Everything else is processed by your authorised dealer bank.

## Annual compliance

- Annual activity certificate for the year to 31 March, certified by a CA, to the bank and the income-tax department (International Taxation).

- Liaison offices: the annual statement to the income-tax department — Form 162 under the Income-tax Rules, 2026 (formerly Form 49C), due within eight months of the year end.

- Branch and project offices: audited accounts, income-tax return, transfer pricing and GST as applicable.

## A change on the way

RBI published draft regulations in October 2025 that would drop the profit and net-worth tests in favour of a list of prohibited activities. Until they are notified, the rules above apply.

## Office or subsidiary?

Most foreign companies that plan to sell in India choose a subsidiary — it’s taxed at a lower rate and limits liability. Compare options in the structure chooser.

## Sources

- RBI Master Direction — branch, liaison and project offices
- Income Tax Department — Form 162 FAQs
- Vinod Kothari — RBI draft branch/office regulations (Oct 2025)

## Frequently asked questions
What is the difference between a liaison office and a branch office in India?
A liaison office is only a communication channel and cannot earn income; a branch office can carry on permitted commercial activities and is taxed as a foreign company. A branch needs five years of profits and USD 100,000 net worth; a liaison office three years and USD 50,000.

How long is a liaison office valid in India?
Generally three years (two years for NBFCs and construction/development companies). The authorised dealer bank can extend it, provided annual activity certificates have been filed.

What replaced Form 49C?
From tax year 2026-27, a liaison office files its annual statement in Form 162 under the Income-tax Rules, 2026, within eight months of the end of the year.

Does a liaison office pay tax in India?
It should have no income, so normally no tax — but it must file annual statements with the income-tax department and an annual activity certificate with its bank.

Please note: this guide is general information based on the rules as they stood on the review date above. Regulations and RBI/CBDT procedures change often — please get advice on your specific facts before acting.

Hiring guide

# Hiring in India without an entity — and the tax risk nobody mentions

An employer of record solves payroll in a week. It doesn’t solve permanent establishment risk. Here’s how foreign companies hire in India safely as they grow.

By CA Durgesh Chavda·Last reviewed 14 October 2026·6 min read

Review your PE risk
hello@durgeshchavda.com

Key takeaways
- Employer of record arrangements are lawful in India.
- An EOR does not remove permanent-establishment risk if staff conclude contracts or work from premises at your disposal.
- Most companies move to a cost-plus subsidiary once the team grows past about ten people.

## Your three options

| Independent contractor | Employer of record (EOR) | Own subsidiary | 

Speed | Days | About 1–2 weeks | 1–2 months | 

Who employs them? | Nobody — a service contract | The EOR, which bills you | Your Indian company | 

Main risk | Misclassification; PE | PE; EOR seen as a sham if you control everything | Compliance workload | 

Usually fits | Genuinely independent specialists | First hires, market testing | Teams of roughly 10+, or long-term plans | 

## Is an employer of record legal in India?

Yes. India has no specific EOR law; it operates as a staffing arrangement, now within the four Labour Codes in force since 21 November 2025. The EOR runs payroll, provident fund, gratuity and statutory filings. What it can’t do is change how the tax authorities see your business.

## Permanent establishment: the real risk

- Dependent agent: India-based staff who habitually conclude contracts or negotiate prices for you can make you taxable in India. Keep signing and pricing authority outside India.

- Service PE: your people providing services in India beyond the treaty’s day threshold (for example 90 days under the India–US treaty) can create a PE.

- Fixed place: after the Supreme Court’s 2025 Hyatt ruling, premises at your disposal can be enough — you needn’t own or lease them.

- If a PE exists, India taxes the profit attributable to it — at foreign-company rates — and expects a return.

## How to stay safe

- Write clear role descriptions: support, engineering and research rather than sales closing.

- Keep contracts approved and signed abroad; avoid giving Indian staff authority to bind you.

- Track days of visiting staff against treaty thresholds.

- Move to a subsidiary with a cost-plus transfer-pricing model once the team is growing — the subsidiary then employs everyone and your PE risk falls sharply.

Need a review of your current set-up? See India tax for foreign companies, or set up properly with company setup in India.

## Sources

- HSF Kramer — India's Labour Codes implemented
- Treelife — permanent establishment risk in India
Related: paying Indian freelancers.

## Frequently asked questions
Can a US company hire an employee in India without an entity?
Yes, through an employer of record or, for genuinely independent work, a contractor agreement. Both are lawful, but neither removes permanent establishment risk if Indian staff conclude contracts or the business operates from India.

Does using an EOR in India create a permanent establishment?
It can. An EOR handles employment, but if the workers habitually conclude contracts for you, provide services beyond treaty day limits or work from premises at your disposal, the tax authorities can treat you as having a PE.

When should a foreign company set up a subsidiary instead of using an EOR?
Usually once the team passes roughly ten people, includes sales or leadership roles, or is planned for the long term. A subsidiary with a cost-plus arrangement reduces PE risk and is often cheaper at scale.

Please note: this guide is general information based on the rules as they stood on the review date above. Regulations and RBI/CBDT procedures change often — please get advice on your specific facts before acting.

Foreign parent guide

# Getting profits out of your Indian subsidiary

“How do we get profit out of our India subsidiary, and what is withheld?” is one of the most common questions from foreign CFOs. Here are the routes, the tax on each and the paperwork.

By CA Durgesh Chavda·Last reviewed 14 October 2026·6 min read

Plan your repatriation
hello@durgeshchavda.com

Key takeaways
- Dividends to a foreign company: 20% plus surcharge and cess, or the lower treaty rate with a TRC and Form 41.
- Service fees and royalties are deductible in India if at arm's length, but carry withholding.
- From 1 April 2026, buybacks are taxed as capital gains rather than dividends.

## The five routes

Route | Deductible for the Indian company? | Indian withholding (domestic) | 

Dividend | No — paid from post-tax profit | 20% plus surcharge and cess | 

Service / management fee | Yes, if at arm’s length and the service is real | Fees for technical services 20%; often nil or 10–15% under treaties | 

Royalty / licence fee | Yes, if at arm’s length | 20%; usually 10–15% under treaties | 

Interest on an intercompany loan | Yes, within interest-limitation rules | Depends on the loan; treaty rates commonly 10–15% | 

Buyback of shares | No | Capital gains in the parent’s hands from 1 April 2026 | 

## Dividend withholding by country

Parent company in | Treaty rate on dividends | 

United States | 15% with 10%+ of voting stock; otherwise 25% | 

United Kingdom | 10% (15% in some cases) | 

Singapore | 10% with 25%+ shareholding; otherwise 15% | 

UAE, Japan, Germany, Netherlands | 10% | 

No treaty / documents missing | 20% plus surcharge and cess | 

Treaty rates need a tax residency certificate, Form 41 and beneficial ownership of the dividend; anti-abuse rules (the MLI principal purpose test) can deny them. Check the treaty and its protocols for your case.

## The paperwork for every remittance

- From the parent: a tax residency certificate, Form 41 (formerly 10F) and, for fees and royalties, a no-PE declaration.

- From the Indian company: withholding under section 393(2), Form 145 online and a CA certificate in Form 146 where required, then the bank remittance.

- Board approvals for dividends; intercompany agreements and transfer-pricing support for fees, royalties and interest; ECB rules for loans.

## Choosing the mix

- Dividends are simple but come from post-tax profit; fees and royalties reduce Indian tax but invite transfer-pricing scrutiny.

- Withholding on fees can often be credited in the parent’s country — check your foreign tax credit position.

- Since April 2026, buybacks are taxed as capital gains (on the gain, not the whole payout) — worth modelling against a dividend.

We handle this for foreign parents — see Indian subsidiary compliance. US parent? Read the India–US tax treaty guide.

## Sources

- Income-tax Act, 2025 — section 207 (Taxsutra)
- Income Tax Department — Form 41 note
- Vinod Kothari — buyback taxation (Feb 2026)

## Frequently asked questions
How much tax is withheld on dividends paid to a foreign parent from India?
20% plus surcharge and cess under domestic law, reduced by the treaty — for example 15% for a US parent holding at least 10%, and 10% for UK, UAE, Japanese, German or Dutch parents — with a tax residency certificate and Form 41.

Can an Indian subsidiary pay management fees to its foreign parent?
Yes, if the services are real, priced at arm's length and documented. Withholding applies under section 393(2), often at a reduced treaty rate, and the fees are deductible for the Indian company.

How are share buybacks taxed in India from 2026?
From 1 April 2026 buyback proceeds are taxed as capital gains in the shareholder's hands — on the gain, after deducting cost — rather than as dividends. Promoters face additional tax.

Is there a limit on repatriating profits from India?
There is no cap on repatriating dividends from profits on which tax has been paid, provided company-law requirements are met and the remittance is documented with the bank.

Please note: this guide is general information based on the rules as they stood on the review date above. Regulations and RBI/CBDT procedures change often — please get advice on your specific facts before acting.
